parsed_answer.content:
In standard Java memory management, the Garbage Collector (GC) automatically reclaims objects when they are deemed unreachable according to strong reference chains. However, enterprise applications often demand finer-grained lifecycle control over cached data, object resurrection, and resource cleanup callbacks without triggering premature OutOfMemoryErrors. This is where java.lang.ref package mechanics come into play, introducing three specialized reference types: Soft, Weak, and Phantom references. Each reference type encapsulates a distinct reachability level, offering varying degrees of interaction with the JVM garbage collector.

Soft references are designed primarily for memory-sensitive caches. An object with a SoftReference will be cleared by the garbage collector only when the JVM is running low on heap memory, just prior to throwing an OutOfMemoryError. This makes them significantly more durable than strong references while still preventing permanent memory bloat. Weak references, conversely, offer zero resistance to the garbage collector. An object that is only weakly reachable will be collected during the very next GC cycle, regardless of current heap utilization. This characteristic forms the foundation of data structures like WeakHashMap, where keys are automatically evicted when no longer referenced elsewhere. Finally, phantom references represent the weakest form of reachability. A PhantomReference is never used to access the referenced object; its get() method always returns null. Instead, phantom references are enqueued into a ReferenceQueue precisely when their underlying referent has been finalized and cleared from memory, making them the industry-standard mechanism for performing deterministic, post-mortem resource cleanup and tracking native memory deallocations.

rows: Only when JVM is low on memory (OOM prevention)
Every GC cycle if no strong references exist
After object is finalized and ready for reclamation

items: Soft references are cleared by the garbage collector globally across the entire heap before the JVM throws an OutOfMemoryError, typically adhering to an LRU-like heuristic maintained by the collector implementation.

Weak references are heavily utilized in the internal mechanics of ThreadLocal and WeakHashMap to prevent memory leaks caused by lingering entry keys when user code loses its direct pointer to the key instance.
Phantom references must be paired with a ReferenceQueue upon instantiation; otherwise, the reference object is useless because it will never be enqueued for polling.

The lifecycle of a phantom-referenced object involves clearing the referent, enqueuing the phantom reference, and only then allowing the memory space of the referent to be reclaimed during subsequent GC phases.

parsed_answer.content: A common production gotcha with Soft and Weak references is assuming that calling System.gc() immediately flushes them. GC is non-deterministic, and relying on it for application logic is a critical architectural anti-pattern. Furthermore, never attempt to resurrect an object inside a finalizer or via a SoftReference revival trick; modern JVMs heavily discourage finalization, and object resurrection leads to convoluted, brittle state machines.
